items.notes: B021 strict-range PASS — Hays, Williamson, Bell. Diagnostic priority: Start with scale and the ligule. Lindheimer muhly is a large dense fountain-form bunchgrass, commonly around 1 m or more tall, with unusually long conspicuous membranous ligules and a tall feathery panicle. items.notes: B021 strict-range PASS — Hays, Williamson, Travis. Diagnostic priority: Start with plant size and blade texture. Seep muhly is a compact upright bunchgrass, usually about 40–80 cm, with threadlike involute leaves and a delicate open panicle that often develops a reddish cast. It is much smaller than Lindheimer muhly but still truly tufted, unlike creeping nimblewill.

items.notes: B021 strict-range PASS — Hays, Travis, Williamson. Diagnostic priority: Forget the ornamental-muhly silhouette: nimblewill is low and weak. That creeping/rooting habit separates it instantly from the two upright bunchgrasses.

items.notes: B022 PASS — Travis, Williamson, Kerr. Diagnostic priority: Start with flower size and the leaf node. Prairie penstemon has enormous pale lavender-to-white flowers, usually about 35–55 mm long, and opposite serrate stem leaves that are sessile and often fused across the node. The calyx and inflorescence are glandular-hairy, and the throat is abruptly inflated.

items.notes: B022 PASS — Hays, Kerr, Bandera. Diagnostic priority: Start with the glossy leaves and the narrower pink-to-red corolla. Hill Country penstemon is an erect perennial with opposite dark-green leaves; lower leaves are often toothed while upper leaves become smaller and more entire/connate. Flowers are usually about 25–35 mm, distinctly smaller than P. cobaea.
items.reconciliation_note: Installed under user blanket approval through species-merge-029-penstemon-b022.

items.notes: B022 UNRESOLVED — Texas native, but fewer than 3 exact project target-zone counties verified. Diagnostic priority: Start with scale and habitat. The calyx lobes are small and sharply pointed, and the exserted staminode carries orange hairs distally.

items.notes: B022 PASS — Val Verde, Edwards, Bandera. Diagnostic priority: Start with the woody base and leaf texture. items.notes: B025 PASS — Hays, Travis, Williamson. Diagnostic priority: Flip the leaf first. Mustang grape has a dense white-to-rusty woolly tomentum on the lower surface that essentially hides the blade surface and veins. items.notes: B025 PASS — Hays, Kerr, Bexar. Diagnostic priority: Start with the lower leaf surface and fruit bloom. Berlandier/Heller's grape has a lower leaf surface that remains visible—sparsely webby/hairy to nearly glabrous—not a solid white felt. Branchlets are slightly angled and usually lack red-banded nodes; ripe berries are conspicuously glaucous and the fruiting clusters are comparatively short and compact.

B025 UNRESOLVED — current taxon concept does not have 3 exact target-zone counties locked. Diagnostic priority: Look at the stem before the fruit. Catbird grape has uniformly red, purplish-red or chestnut branchlets and usually deeply 3(–5)-lobed leaves with long-pointed lobes. The lower leaf surface is essentially glabrous, and it is a riverbank/slough/floodplain grape.
